newsitem.title: UK: Virgin pledges annual cargo rate rise policy.
newsitem.headline: Virgin pledges annual cargo rate rise policy.

text.p: Virgin Atlantic Cargo has issued a promise to its shipper and freight forwarder customers that unless unusual circumstances prevail it will in future only raise its rates once a year, in the spring.
In the past, Virgin and most other carriers have "adjusted" -- airfreight industry terminology for increased -- their cargo rates twice yearly, in the spring and autumn.

"Shippers and forwarders have told us that they would prefer just one annual increase because that would help them with their long-term strategic planning and I see no reason why we can't comply with their wishes," David Woodward, Virgin Atlantic Cargo's general manager commercial, told Reuters.

"This would especially help forwarders who often have to negotiate contracts with their clients a year in advance. There is an argument that once-a-year rate increases should be higher than the level of the twice-yearly rises but because of the advantages that would result, I think our customers would accept that," he said.
Virgin Atlantic Cargo increased its rates by an average of three to seven percent from April 1.
Woodward stressed that rate increases would always incorporate fluctuations in the price of jet fuel.

He defended the decision by the vast majority of carriers to impose a surcharge equivalent to six U.S. cents per kg last October/November in the wake of rapidly rising fuel costs, even though shippers and agents expressed dismay at receiving little or no notice.
"Despite claims by some of our customers, there was no collusion amongst airlines to suddenly introduce the surcharge at the same time," he said.

"We had all sat and watched as fuel prices went up and up and we all realised that something had to be done about the situation. What it required was a major player in the market -- it turned out to be Lufthansa -- to impose a surcharge for the rest to follow," he said.
Woodward said that if Virgin was ever again confronted with similar circumstances and felt another fuel surcharge was required, he would like to give shippers and forwarders more notice.
"But we would ask for loyalty and understanding in return," he said.

"When we introduced the surcharge last time, we did it about two weeks earlier than some other carriers and in that fortnight we lost customers to them. I felt that was a pretty short-sighted approach (on behalf of the shippers and agents who moved their business elsewhere)," he said.
Virtually all airlines removed their surcharges last month as fuel prices fell to what they considered more reasonable levels.
